problem: LLM-based robot planners need an accurate, up-to-date scene representation, but prior scene-graph approaches (SayPlan, DELTA, SayNav, ConceptGraphs) rely on heavy VLM/vision models that are hard to update in real time. Noisy mask-based object localization also gives imprecise 3D positions in dynamic scenes.
motivation: Assistive and human-robot interaction settings change constantly because of human actions, so plans generated by an LLM misalign with reality without a continuously refreshed semantic map. A lightweight scene-graph generator (PSGTR, about 400 ms per 480p frame on a T4) plus temporal filtering could give real-time, reliable state tracking.
key_idea: Build and continuously update a semantic room/object scene graph from RGB-D frames with a lightweight panoptic scene-graph model (PSGTR), and refine object 3D positions with a particle filter using IoU-based mask association and camera-motion prediction, so an LLM planner works from an up-to-date map.
insight: Filtering noisy per-frame centroid estimates over time markedly reduces localization error. In the 30-measurement comparison, mean absolute error goes from (0.07, 0.18, 0.02) m to (0.02, 0.02, 0.01) m, and error std roughly halves. A cheap, less accurate segmenter is workable for real-time use when temporal filtering compensates for its noise. Evidence is limited to this single small table.
method: Perception input: RGB-D frames plus camera pose relative to the geometric map are fed to PSGTR to get object masks, labels, and pairwise relationship labels with probabilities.

Semantic map: a directed graph with room nodes (from the geometric map) and object nodes (3D position, category, size), with edges for object relations, room connectivity, and object-to-room membership.

Node/edge construction: mask centroids are back-projected from pixel to camera to map coordinates. A distance filter prunes far objects, and edges are created only if both endpoints pass the distance check and the relation probability exceeds a threshold.
Data association: the previous mask is warped by the camera motion ΔT = T_t T_{t-1}^{-1}, and IoU with the current masks is thresholded (λ_IoU) to match objects across frames.

Particle filter: N particles per object are initialised from a Gaussian around the first observation. Prediction applies the camera transform plus noise. Weights are 1/(1+Euclidean distance to the new observation), normalised, and the position estimate is the weighted mean. Unmatched observations start new objects.

Planner module (only outlined): Task Planner, Skill Planner, Executor, Controller and Explainer consume the semantic scene to turn natural-language requests into skills (GOTO, PICK, PLACE) and replan on failure. It is deployed on the RoBee humanoid.

setting.backbone: PSGTR (pretrained panoptic scene graph transformer) + particle filter; LLM planner (unspecified, details deferred)
setting.training_data: Pretrained PSGTR used as is; no new training reported
setting.observation: RGB-D camera frames plus camera pose relative to the geometric map
setting.action_space: High-level skills (GOTO, PICK, PLACE) decomposed into low-level executable actions
setting.privileged: Known geometric map and robot/camera pose (localization); room nodes derived from the geometric map

numbers_note: No navigation benchmark results. The only quantitative result is a 30-measurement object position error comparison with and without the particle filter (Table 1), which is not a benchmark metric.
results: On 30 position measurements of one object, the particle filter cut mean absolute error from (0.07, 0.18, 0.02) m to (0.02, 0.02, 0.01) m and error std from (0.35, 0.24, 0.03) to (0.17, 0.12, 0.02). No end-to-end task or navigation benchmark results are reported, and no baselines are compared.
limitations: Evaluation is minimal: one object, 30 measurements, and no end-to-end planning or navigation results or baseline comparisons.
The planner is not described (deferred to another article), so the LLM-driven claims are unsupported here.
PSGTR gives coarse panoptic segmentation, and the method relies on a known geometric map and accurate camera poses.
